# Porting techniques

Recipes for the traps listed in `SKILL.md`. Each says when it applies, what to
do, and what it did the last time.

## Build-time patch

When: the hack's own constants make it too big for the board. Maze keeps a
1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one `calloc`, about
20 MB, and the board has 8 MB of PSRAM.

- The copy in `hacks/<name>/` stays byte-identical to upstream (`cmp` it).
- A PlatformIO `pre:` script (`firmware/patch_maze.py`) writes a patched copy
  into the build directory, using a tested function (`tools/maze_patch.py`)
  that raises if upstream's lines change. A wrapper (`hacks/maze_small.c`)
  includes that copy, and the original is excluded in `build_src_filter` of
  all three environments (`stopwatch`, `native`, `dump`).
- Maze's limits went from 1000 to 80: about 125 KB.
- A patch can switch off a branch (Pacman's `NRAND (2) == 0` becomes `0`) or
  replace a whole function (its route search becomes a loop). Check the
  original's SHA-256 so an upstream edit fails the build. Before a rewrite, pin
  a long-run fingerprint taken with the original (30,000 frames, every ghost's
  position every 100), show the code ran, and mutate the order to watch the pin
  fail.

## Single precision

When: a hot loop does `double` maths or calls `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt` or `pow`.
The ESP32-S3 has a single-precision FPU only, so double runs in software.

- Find the hot loop first and count the calls. Substrate makes four `sin` calls
  per sand grain, with 64 grains a crack and up to 100 cracks: about 25,000
  software `sin`s a frame. Its step grew from 5 ms to 121 ms as the picture
  filled.
- Wrapper `hacks/<name>_single.c`: include the framework headers first, then
  `hacks/single_precision.h`, then the unmodified hack. Exclude the original in
  `build_src_filter` of all three environments.
- `M_PI` is a double literal, so the angle arithmetic stays double: put
  `#undef M_PI` and a float definition after the header. Literals such as
  `0.81` stay double too, and a header cannot change them: `0.5 * x` with a
  float `x` is software double maths. Check the wrapper's object for soft-double
  helpers with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm braid.o | grep ' U __.*df'` (compile with
  `-Os -mlongcalls` and the shim's include paths). If any remain, rewrite the
  literals at build time as Braid does: `tools/float_literals.py` (tested, skips
  strings and comments) run by `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, and the
  wrapper includes `<name>_floatlit.c` from the build directory. GCC's
  `-fsingle-precision-constant` does the same, but Apple clang ignores it, so
  host tests would run other arithmetic than the board.
- Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame and Substrate were wrapped before this check
  and now go through it too, with `single_constants.h` (`MAXRAND`, `M_PI`) and
  `single_frand.h`. Run `uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>` on the
  wrapper's object after `pio run -e stopwatch`: any count in a per-frame
  function means a literal, macro or `double` struct field the rename missed
  (`x11shim.md` has the four that did). A trig argument that is a big whole
  number is a fifth: look at a frame before trusting the float build.
- A plain single-precision wrapper is cheap to try: include
  `single_precision.h`, `single_constants.h` and `<name>_floatlit.c`, exclude
  the original in the three `build_src_filter` lines and list the name in
  `patch_float_literals.py`. Measure it on the board and drop it if it moves
  nothing. On the board, step before to after: Hopalong 7-20 to 3.4 ms,
  WhirlWindWarp 6-26 to 3.8 ms, BinaryHorizon 95.8 to 31.8 ms, Barcode 77.1 to
  56.1 ms (frames byte-identical), XSpirograph 44.2 to 10.9 ms, Vines 182 to
  10.3 ms; Bouboule stayed at 14.5 ms.
- Hand-written `sin` and `cos` (`hacks/fast_trig.h`) moved Braid by 5%. Do the
  literals first.
- Compare double and float frames at several counts. Early frames match; a
  chaotic hack diverges later but should keep its look.
- GL hacks too: Hypnowheel's spiral called `cos` and `sin` in `double` for
  every vertex, about 275 ms of a 706 ms step, hidden behind a fill-heavy look.
  Its wrapper (`hypnowheel_single_gl.c`) adapts `get_position` and
  `get_rotation` as HexTrail's does.
- Results: Galaxy 5 to 14 fps. Substrate step 119-121 ms to 37-38 ms, 6.2 to
  12.5 fps.
- A hack that passes the address of its own `double` local to a shim function
  (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &s, &v)`) writes eight bytes into a four-byte float, and
  the compiler does not warn. Moire's frames were all different from the
  double build's until `moire_single.c` mapped the call to an adapter defined
  before `single_precision.h`. Cmp the wrapper's frames against the unmodified
  hack's. A hack with no decimal literals must stay out of
  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses it.
- Once the maths is float, look at the fills before the next idea. CWaves'
  cosines were 4 ms of a 61 ms step; its 233 column fills were 57 (a thin
  full-height rectangle touches a new cache line a store). See `hacks.md`.
- A float build can break a check that held in double. Both the S3 (`madd.s`)
  and arm64 fuse a multiply and an add, so `t*n - floor(t*n)` uses the exact
  product for the subtraction and the rounded one for the `floor`, and can
  come out slightly negative: Celtic's `assert(tt>=0 && tt<1)` aborted at
  t 0.331093 with 3422 segments. The 3000-frame test (`pio test`) found it
  on the host, and the same abort would have hit the board. Compute the
  product once in a build-time patch (`tools/celtic_patch.py`). Map any libm
  call the hack makes that `single_precision.h` does not (`rint`, `floor`),
  and check the object with `nm` for `__*df*` helpers, not only `__muldf3`.

## Slow hack

When: a ported hack runs under about 10 fps and the push is not the cause
(`step` in the serial line is large).

- For a GL hack, flash a `-DGL_PROFILE` build first (AGENTS.md): it splits
  the frame into stages, and time in none of them is the hack's own code.
  Issue #73 guessed Hypnowheel was 70 percent blended fill; the profile showed
  a third of its frame was `double` trig.
- A worst-case microbenchmark is not the workload. A PSRAM cache miss costs
  about 220 cycles, which suggested GL fill was memory-bound; a banded renderer
  in internal RAM, built on that, was exact and slower (neighbouring triangles
  share cache lines). A/B the first working slice of a speed idea on the board
  before building the rest, and stop if it does not pay.
- Do not trust a host profile (`sample` on the dump program) for where the
  time goes. A Mac does `double` at full speed, so software-double code looks
  cheap there: Braid's disc fill was 6% on the host and the largest cost on the
  board.
- Split the step on the device with a temporary build flag that makes the
  expensive call return at once (Braid: `XDrawLine`). The step left is the
  hack's own cost; the difference is the drawing. Remove the flag before
  committing.
- Count what is called per frame (segments, calls, rows) before guessing,
  and look at the object file for soft-double helpers (see "Single precision").
- Change one thing, pin that the pixels did not move (`cmp` frames at several
  counts, or the pinned hash), flash, and compare second windows. Braid's four
  changes were worth 2.7-3.2 times, 1.05, and 1.3.
- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1) are the costly path: a quad filled a row at
  a time, plus two discs for round caps. `stroke.c` keeps a table of disc rows
  by width up to 16. A wide full circle through `XDrawArc` is about a thousand
  such segments (Deluxe: 94% of a frame, 2-5 fps); `stroke_circle` fills it as
  a ring in two spans a row.
- When the cost is overpaint, not `double` maths, a host split does find the
  dominant call: `#define XDrawArc(...) 0` in the wrapper, `pio run -e dump`,
  then `/usr/bin/time -p .pio/build/dump/program <index> 400 out.raw` three
  times, against the baseline. It cannot see costs that live in memory
  traffic (Deluxe's alpha mask: nothing on the host, 3-5 ms on the board).
- Counting works where timing misleads: a scratch copy of the hack with a
  counter in the inner function and a macro round `XDrawLine` gave Celtic's
  spline evaluations and line draws per draw call on the host, by graph type.
  A cost per eval and per line fitted to a first device capture (about 1.7 us
  and 22 us, from three graph types and a handful of windows) estimated 63 ms
  for the biggest type after the change; the next capture's 12.6-76.8 ms did
  not contradict it, but the log does not say which type each window was, so
  the fit is unchecked.
- A hack's own pacing constants can be the lever: Celtic's 0.0001 tick (a
  patch scales it, `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE`) set both the look-ahead's work and how
  many draw calls a picture takes. Count the draw calls a picture takes and
  the pause after it before reading `fps=`: with a 5 s pause the column read
  5.2 in every window and measured the pause, not the drawing. Use
  `1000 / (step + push + delay)` for the drawing rate.
- Heap and speed were two problems in Celtic and one fix cured only the
  first: the graph sized to the screen cut a pattern's heap about 9 times and
  left spline evaluations per call unchanged. Measure both after each change.
- A hack that redraws its whole picture every frame to animate colour (Braid)
  costs its full draw each frame whatever the push does. Check this before
  porting; the scorer does not flag it yet.
- A fix that moves the frame rate by under 5% shows the maths was not the
  cost. HexTrail in single precision went from 12.7 to 13.0 fps; the 2.3 fps
  that mattered came from reading what the GL layer does each frame
  (`glshim_clear`) and finding a depth clear that nothing read, because the hack
  never enables the depth test. Run `nm` on the object, then read the shared
  code the hack calls before trying a third idea in the hack.
- A step that grows over the hack's cycle (HexTrail: 19 ms to a ceiling, then it
  restarts) needs the worst window, not the mean. Capture at least one full
  cycle (150 s covered HexTrail's 65 s), read the lowest `fps=`, and compare the
  time spent below 10 fps with the rotation interval: Rod saw it fall under 10
  before the 25 s change. If a resource such as `count` scales the cost, give it
  an `#ifndef` default in `registry.c` (`HEXTRAIL_COUNT`) so one flash tests
  another value, and measure two or three values: count 6 gave a mean of 12.7,
  10 gave 9.1 and 20 gave 5.7, in double precision.
- Before writing a speed override, grep the hack's header and glue for the
  author's own knob (`GLB_SLOW_GL` in `bubble3d.h`, set from the wrapper with
  `#undef` and `#define` after the header). It keeps the copy byte-identical
  and is the trade the author intended: Bubble3D went from 4-5 fps to a mean
  of 11.4. A hack split over several files (entry point in one, work in
  another) gets one `<name>_*gl.c` wrapper per file, and only the file that
  does the maths needs `single_precision.h`.

## Thin lines in a GL hack

When: a GL hack draws hairlines or fades (Unknown Pleasures) and looks right
in a host frame but flickers on the board. Work down this list, one layer at a
time, and look at the screen (or film) after each; each layer hid the next.

- Lines hop. TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel, so a drifting line
  jumps. `tinygl_patch.py` keeps the fractional position and draws a Wu line
  when the hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Triangles are still snapped.
- Quads that hide the lines behind them hide nothing, or the picture is
  speckled grey. TinyGL's blend adds colours, ignores alpha and misreads our
  byte-swapped pixels, so `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA` is drawn as an
  opaque fill. Smooth lines carry no alpha, so a hack's per-line fade is lost.
- A line drawn on its own polygon's edge is erased in dashes: `glPolygonOffset`
  was stored and never read. The patch applies it, plus a margin for the
  vertex snapping. Check the effect on the host by the second difference of a
  frame's total brightness while the picture drifts a fraction of a pixel; change
  one thing at a time, because blending once made the experiment unable to
  show any effect.
- Pieces of a line vanish for one refresh. The panel scans while the push
  writes, so a seam crosses the picture. Set `sync_to_refresh` on the hack
  (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`); see `.claude/rules/device-display.md` for the
  offset, why it is only valid for a full-frame push, and how to film the
  result. Cost: up to a refresh of latency a frame, so only a hack that needs
  it should ask.
- Budget with `gl_budget.py` but expect it to be off: it has no blend term
  (Unknown Pleasures was predicted at 251 ms and ran at 267, then 197 once the
  fills were opaque). Add the measured row as a calibration point.
- After all that a dimming of about 14% for 25 ms at each push remained (issue
  #68). Do not promise a hack is flicker-free from a host frame or from the
  absence of vanishing lines alone.

## Stack check

When: locals over a few KB. Compile the hack with `-O1 -fstack-usage` (flags in
AGENTS.md) and keep each frame well under the 16 KB loop stack. Host tests
cannot see an overflow: Rorschach's 9.6 KB array rebooted the device on its
first frame, and only the serial log's "Stack canary" showed it.

Recursion: replay it, don't guess. Run the hack on a pthread with a painted
1 MB stack over several seeds and thousands of frames (Pacman's generator: 236
KB median, 315 KB worst; `ulimit -s` saw only the first, shallow level). Read a
frame's size from the ELF (`xtensa-esp32s3-elf-objdump -d`, `entry a1, N`), and
decode a panic backtrace with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-addr2line` against an ELF
rebuilt with the same flags. A recursion over a grid is bounded by its cells:
replay it from every start.

## Large allocations

When: one allocation of 100 KB or more, or the hack calls `exit()` if it fails.

- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so host leak
  numbers are double the device's.
- Plain `malloc` and `realloc` of two 868 KB buffers (Substrate) landed in
  PSRAM: free PSRAM fell by 1,742,096 bytes, which is 2 x 466 x 466 x 4 plus a
  few KB. Internal heap barely moved.
- On restart the buffers were freed and allocated again, and free PSRAM
  returned to the same value. Read heap and PSRAM in the log to confirm this
  for each large hack.

## Images

Colour pixmaps are canvases: every drawing primitive, `XCopyArea` and
`XCopyPlane` draw into them. Bitmaps take only `XCopyArea` from another
bitmap. There is no PNG
decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads a raw RGB565 blob and
mask (format in `ximage-loader.h`), made by `tools/make_logo_blob.py`.
`XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repository root) swaps the logo for a local
image at build time. Keep a third-party logo under `vendor/`, out of git.

A big blob (Pacman's is 3 MB as C text) is built from `vendor/` by a `pre:`
script and never committed; write it to a `.partial` file and rename it.

## Pixmap double buffering

When: a plain screenhack makes two pixmaps, draws into them and `XCopyArea`s the
result to the window (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes, Halftone,
Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole). Since #61 this works as copied, but a back
buffer costs 434 KB of PSRAM and a full-frame copy each frame, and dirties
every row, so the push loses what the dirty rectangle (#52) saves. Draw
straight on the canvas instead, as below. (These eight were ported before #61,
when the copy from a blank pixmap erased the picture.)

- A pinned hash of a blank frame passes silently (`0xa4f79500bd791711ull`, which
  is also Pedal's at frame 200). Look at the frame before pinning.
- Upstream switches the buffering off under `HAVE_JWXYZ` ("Don't second-guess
  Quartz's double-buffering"), or reads a `doubleBuffer` resource. Write
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c`: include `screenhack.h` and the math headers, empty
  `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, `#define HAVE_JWXYZ`, include the unmodified hack and
  register its `HackEntry`. Exclude the original from `build_src_filter` in all
  three environments. `grep HAVE_JWXYZ` first: Interaggregate also uses it for
  pixel packing, but only in the 24 and 32 bit cases, and the canvas is 16 bit.
- A hack that uses a pixmap as storage needs no wrapper. Truchet draws a canvas
  bigger than the window into an 866 by 866 pixmap (1.5 MB of PSRAM) and
  scrolls it with `XCopyArea` offsets.

## Restart leak test

When: the hack restarts itself. Override its cycle resource in the test (for
example `*maxCycles: 3`), compare `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`
before and after many restarts, and prove the test sees a leak by removing a
`free` in a temporary copy or leaking from a shim function. Never leave the
hack changed: `cmp` it afterwards.

Measure the growth first, then set the tolerance just above it (Pacman: exactly
0, so 512 bytes). A loose one passes a leaked GC; mutation-check by leaking one.

On the device, work out how long a restart takes: cycles times the frame time.
Substrate's 10,000 cycles at about 160 ms is 27 minutes, and the restart showed
at about 25. Capture that long, with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`.

## Stopping before the first draw

When: the hack allocates on its first `draw` (look for a lazy `initted` flag)
but sizes its `free` from values set in `init`. Two quick button presses, or a
press with the 90 s rotation, free a hack before it has drawn once. Blaster
sets `NUM_ROBOTS` in init, allocates `robots` in draw, and its free loops over
`robots[i].lasers`, so freeing it first dereferenced NULL. The dump tool with 0
frames exited 139.

- `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame` starts and stops every
  hack with no frame, so a new port that has this problem fails the host suite.
- To fix it without editing the hack, write a wrapper that includes the
  unmodified source with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers the hack
  itself, with a `free` that makes the loop safe (`hacks/blaster_safe.c`).
- A real press is rarely handled in that window: Rod's presses on the device
  all landed after the first step. Rely on the test, not on pressing buttons.
- An xlockmore hack cannot be re-registered that way: `xlockmore.h` has no
  include guard, so the hack's own include redefines `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`
  after the wrapper empties it. Swap the callback in the table instead, from a
  constructor: `<name>_xlockmore_function_table.hack_init = my_init;`
  (`loop_direct.c`, `hypnowheel_single_gl.c`).

## Tests that cannot be fooled

A test that runs a real hack can pass for the wrong reason. Pyro clears its own
window in `init`, so a "starts black" test through Pyro passed with the runner
deliberately broken. Test shared runner behaviour with stub hacks
(`test_runner_xsft.c`) and mutate the code to see the test fail.

A check can also be true before the hack has run. "At least 20 non-black
pixels" proved a hack drew, until Substrate started on a white canvas and
passed without drawing at all. Compare with the canvas as the hack started, and
keep a stub hack that draws nothing, on the colour that fooled the old check, to
show the test can fail. When a change alters what every hack starts with (the
background colour, an initial canvas), re-read the older tests that assume the
old start.

A bounds guard can be unreachable through the public API. TinyGL's clipper
keeps a line inside the view volume and its viewport maps that to at most pixel
63.5, so two of the four guards in the smooth-line plot survived mutation until
a test used a viewport bigger than the canvas. Mutate each guard on its own
(a scratchpad script that edits, runs the suite and restores in `finally`),
and when one survives, find an input that reaches it or say it is defensive.
Wrapping bugs can also hide in what is stored, not what is drawn: a depth that
wrapped round only showed when a third fill was drawn afterwards.

## Wrapping an xlockmore hack's init or draw

Emptying `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` (Blaster) fails: the hack includes
`xlockmore.h`, which has no include guard and defines it again. Rename the
hack's tables instead (`#define pipes_xscreensaver_function_table
pipes_upstream_xscreensaver_table`, the same for `_xlockmore_function_table`),
include the hack, `#undef` both, define the wrappers, then
`#define draw_pipes pipes_draw_no_fade` and call
`XSCREENSAVER_MODULE_2("Pipes", pipes, pipes)`. See `hacks/pipes_gl.c`.

## Background colour

The runner paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before `init`,
as `screenhack.c` paints the window. Substrate (`.background: white`) depends
on it. Every earlier hack asks for black or nothing.

## Skipping a hack

Threads and shared memory are not worth porting. Record the name and the
reason in `tools/failed_ports.txt` (`name: reason`); the scorer marks it as
abandoned. Xft text used to be on this list; it is not now (see "Xft text").

## Xft text

A hack that draws with Xft (`XftDrawStringUtf8`, `load_xft_font_retry`) needs
the stand-in in `x11shim/xft.h`. Its font is Special Elite, rasterised at build
time into pixel-coverage tables (`firmware/font_atlas.py`, which runs
`tools/make_font_atlas.py` on the TTF in `firmware/assets/fonts/`), and
`main.cpp` installs it with `xshim_set_font`. Only ASCII has glyphs: anything
else draws as `?`. The family in a font name is ignored and the baked size
nearest the number is used, so to change a hack's text size override its font
resource (XJack's `XJACK_FONT_PX`) and bake the size in `font_atlas.py`.

Our `screenhack.h` does not include `xft.h`, because that would change what
every hack sees. Build the hack through a wrapper that includes it first
(`hacks/xjack_xft.c`), and exclude the original from all three
`build_src_filter` lines. XJack's wrapper shows two things an Xft hack may
need from `screenhack.c`: the window background set from the `background`
resource (`XClearWindow` otherwise clears to black), and a reshape after
init. Tests that run the hack install `test_font.h`'s blocky font, so a
pinned hash does not follow FreeType; with no font installed the shim gives a
blank one, so a test that replays every hack does not abort.

## Worktree setup

A fresh worktree lacks the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/`:
symlink them from the main checkout. They show as untracked, so `git add`
named paths, never `-A`. Adding them to `.git/info/exclude` changes state shared
with every worktree: ask Rod first.

A worktree session refuses `source`, `$VAR` in a command and `&&` chains with a
computed path. Run plain commands with literal paths, for example
`PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio test -e native`.

## Device capture

- Pin the hack with `-DSTART_HACK=\"name\"` and add `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`, or the
  board rotates to the next hack after 90 s.
- Send upload output to a file, never through `head`, and look for "Hash of
  data verified".
- Capture 150 s or more of serial in the background, longer to see a restart.
  Read `step`, `push`, `wait`, heap and PSRAM, and any "Stack canary".
- Compare with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: pushes became
  41-45 ms on every hack after the byte-order fix, against 31 ms before (#23).
- Pinning a frame hash: set the new hack's `kBaseline` entry to `1`, run
  `pio test -f test_hacks`, read `Was N` in the failure and convert with
  `python3 -c "print('0x%016xull' % N)"`. Pin only after looking at the frame
  (and never type the hex by hand: one was wrong).
- Showing Rod a hack: flash `-DSTART_HACK=\"first\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=25` with
  `XS_LOGO=...` so the new ones come up in order, then tell him which, and that
  the button steps backwards (from Pyro it wraps to the last hack).

398	  nothing more. The registry gives it 120 bees and 8 colours. In single
399	  precision its flow dies out within about 600 frames (the screen stays
400	  black), so it is double: 3.0-4.8 fps, about 200 ms of every step being its
401	  search for the next flow. A single frame at 300 frames looked right in
402	  both: sweep several frame counts (300, 1000, 3000) for a hack that
403	  restarts itself or can die out.
404	- CCurve's `*limit` of 200,000 segments (each a malloc and a recursion) took
405	  740 ms in single precision and 2.9 s in double; the wrapper caps it at 30,000.
406	  Its 1.4 fps is its own pacing: 0.4 s between iterations, 42 ms of work.
407	- Droste (`droste_small.c`) hands back a loader token on the first call and
408	  finishes on the next, with the pixmap's size as the rectangle, so upstream's
409	  own "just finished" branch runs. It loads a picture the size of the window,
410	  not 2.5 times it (5.4 MB as the 32-bit image `XGetImage` makes), and renders
411	  at half width and height through `lowrez_put.h` (630 ms became 190 ms, 4.6
412	  fps). `XPutPixel` is mapped to swap the pixel, since `lowrez_put.h` wants
413	  ordinary RGB565 and the picture holds canvas order. MetaBalls takes all but
414	  28 KB of the internal heap while it runs (466 row buffers of 466 bytes).
415	- RotZoomer and Twang (`rotzoomer_single.c`, `twang_single.c`) start their
416	  picture and tiles the first time `draw` finds `load_image_async_simple`
417	  finished. The shim finishes at once and returns NULL, so that branch never
418	  ran and the first draw used a NULL zoom box (exit 139). Each wrapper does
419	  the finishing step straight after init. Changing the shim to return a loader
420	  would also change Boxfit and DecayScreen, so it is Rod's call. Both are
421	  single precision (they call `sin` and `cos` in double for every pixel).
422	  RotZoomer is unpinned in `test_hacks.c`: with no grab image every frame is
423	  black.
424	- BinaryHorizon (`binaryhorizon_swapped.c`) is told the display is 24 bits
425	  deep. Its 16-bit path adds less than a step of a channel per hit and rounds
426	  its random colour walk down, so every colour drifted to black or a dim
427	  green (as in BinaryRing). Pixels go straight to the window, and its image
428	  and pixmap are one pixel big, because nothing reads them. Every 30 s it
429	  restarts and callocs a new pixel buffer without freeing the old one (868 KB
430	  on the device): the wrapper frees it and clears the window.
431	- Munch defaults to `*xor: True`, so `XDrawPoint` honours `GXxor` now (only
432	  that primitive: lines and fills still copy). `pow2.h` is our own
433	  `i_log2` and `to_pow2`. IMSMap needed 1-bit `XYBitmap` images, `BitmapPad`
434	  is 32, and Deco needed `allocate_writable_colors` and `XStoreColors` (no
435	  writable cells). The scorer's gap lists were wrong twice: MetaBalls'
436	  `XListPixmapFormats` is under `#if 0`, and Ant needed only `automata.h`, a
437	  file in `hacks/` that is now copied to `xs_support/`.
438	- NerveRot passes the address of its own `double` locals to `rgb_to_hsv`, so
439	  its single-precision wrapper has an adapter (as Moire's). The restart test
440	  under AddressSanitizer found it as a stack-buffer-overflow, but a host frame
441	  looked right.
442	- Bouboule's upstream default is a red and a blue starfield for 3D glasses,
443	  drawn with `GXor`, which the shim does not do. The registry overrides
444	  `*use3d: False` (a single colour cycling through the palette) and
445	  `*cycles: 0`. Twang's 3 by 3 tiles of 120 pixels leave black margins and
446	  clip at the round bezel; `*tileSize` is the lever.
447	- A wrapper that finishes an image load itself (RotZoomer, Twang, Droste) must
448	  also handle the hack's timed reload, which the shim finishes at once too, so
449	  upstream's "just finished" branch never runs again. It must also match image
450	  layouts: `XGetImage` gives a 32-bit image, and a hack that memcpys it into
451	  its own 16-bit buffer shows alternating black pixels. RotZoomer did on the
452	  board until the trail review caught it. Test with a flat grab image and
453	  assert every pixel, then change the image before a timed restart.
454	- A wrapper that clears state before upstream's own timed check (BinaryHorizon
455	  frees its buffer) reads the clock separately from upstream, and the two reads
456	  can straddle a second. Read it once a frame and route upstream's `time()` to
457	  that reading with a function-like `#define time(p)`; test it with a fake
458	  clock whose second read is later.
459	- A hack that leaks on every in-hack restart (Munch's `get_string_resource`
460	  result) needs a restart-loop leak test of its own: `test_hacks` restarts only
461	  through start and stop.
462	- Deluxe's `draw_star` (ten sin/cos in software `double`, #54 idea 5): a
463	  single-precision build gave identical frames and no device gain (step
464	  45.06 vs 45.12 ms, pinned, 2 rounds). Skip it; the step is the blend, the
465	  mask and the strokes.
466	- Bubble3D is four files (`b_lockglue.c` holds `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, so the
467	  scorer knows it as `b_lockglue`; `SOURCE_STEMS` in `score_hacks.py` maps the
468	  registry name `bubble3d` to it), each built as its own `USE_GL` unit by
469	  `bubble3d_*gl.c`. Only `bubble3d.c` has a licence text; Rod chose to list the
470	  other four under its notice. The glue's `init()` builds a sphere and drops it
471	  (leaked on every start: the wrapper makes that call return NULL). A GL
472	  profile put 220 of a 300-390 ms step in a software-double `cos` per nudge
473	  axis per vertex: `bubble3d_bubble_gl.c` is single precision (frames
474	  byte-identical). Upstream's own `GLB_SLOW_GL` (set in `bubble3d_gl.c`) takes
475	  the sphere from 1,280 to 320 triangles: 4-5 fps became mean 11.5, worst
476	  window 8.2, with the push (12-24 ms, a full frame) now a fifth of the frame.
477	  It is flagged `repaints_all` since the GL layer follows the canvas swap
478	  (issue #118): 11.2 to 12.0 fps, worst window 8.0 to 8.8. Upstream's
479	  default `transparent` skips the depth test and expects a blend TinyGL's fill
480	  does not do, so back faces overwrote front faces as a dark wedge in each
481	  bubble (found by the trail review): the registry overrides `*transparent:
482	  False`, which enables the depth test. It cost nothing measurable on the
483	  board (mean 11.5 before, 11.4 after).
484	- Bubbles (`bubbles_safe.c`, `bubbles_sprites.py`) is three copied files and
485	  44 PNGs (four sets of eleven sizes: blood, blue, glass, jade) that the
486	  pre-script deflates into the build dir with `make_logo_blob.py --deflate`,
487	  never committed. Upstream's free leaks every live bubble in the mesh lists
488	  and one extra step pixmap: the wrapper frees both, and the leak test fails
489	  if either free is removed (checked by mutation). `bubbles.h` includes
490	  `<X11/Xlib.h>`, which the shim now answers with a header that pulls in
491	  `xshim.h`. A host dump always shows the same set, so seed `random()` to see
492	  the others (jade, blue and glass came up in six seeds, blood did not).
493	  Blood is teal with red mottling in the source art, not red: Rod saw cyan
494	  with red spots on the panel and it matches `blood11.png`, so it is not a
495	  byte swap. A single frame can show a bubble with a bite out of it while
496	  neighbours merge and are redrawn; the bite is gone a few frames later. On
497	  the board it ran at 54-62 fps (mean 57.4), a 5-7 ms step under its own
498	  9.5 ms wait, and held nothing in PSRAM: it is paced by its delay, not by the
499	  work.
500	- The 2026-10-18 GL batch (GLMatrix, CubeStack, Kaleidocycle, DangerBall,
501	  Cubenetic, DeepStars, Superquadrics, Menger) is eight `USE_GL` wrappers over
502	  unmodified sources. Most GL hacks wait 20-40 ms after a frame (`*delay`), and
503	  the loop credits only the push against it, so `kShortDelayOverrides` (10 ms)
504	  took CubeStack from 16.5 to 22 fps, Kaleidocycle 19.6 to 33 and DangerBall
505	  16.5 to 25 with no other change. Their motion is per frame, so it is faster
506	  too, nearer upstream's pace on a desktop.
507	- CubeStack (`cubestack_gl.c`) blends `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE` with an alpha of
508	  opacity times each face's transition, and TinyGL ignores vertex alpha: the
509	  wrapper's `glColor4fv` scales its colour (the first frame is black, where
510	  10,883 pixels were lit without it), so the cubes are translucent as upstream
511	  draws them. Upstream wraps its palette index with `>` instead of `>=`, so
512	  after about 12,900 frames it reads `colors[32]` of 32 (an AddressSanitizer
513	  overflow in a 13,500 frame test): the wrapper wraps it before each draw.
514	  Kaleidocycle also blends but its faces are opaque, so it was not folded.
515	- Kaleidocycle starts with `count = 0`, so its first frame computes a piece's
516	  angle as 0 / 0: a NaN that reaches TinyGL's viewport conversion and is cast to
517	  an int (the trail review found it with `-fsanitize=float-cast-overflow`:
518	  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS='-fsanitize=float-cast-overflow
519	  -fno-sanitize-recover=all' pio run -e dump`, then dump one frame).
520	  `tools/kaleidocycle_patch.py` guards the denominator; `kaleidocycle_gl.c`
521	  includes the build's patched copy (`generated/kaleidocycle_patched.c`, written
522	  by `patch_float_literals.py` with no literal pass), and frames are unchanged.
523	- Superquadrics' `myrand` multiplies in `float` (upstream too), so the largest
524	  `LRAND()` rounds up and `myrand(4)` is 4, one past `pats[4][4]`.
525	  `tools/superquadrics_patch.py` clamps it at build time; its test compiles the
526	  real function with `LRAND()` fixed at 2147483647 (the trail review found it).
527	- GLMatrix (`glmatrix_single_gl.c`) keeps its look in alpha: the texture's
528	  alpha is the glyph image's green channel and each glyph's brightness is the
529	  vertex alpha, drawn `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`. TinyGL has none, and the shim's
530	  `glTexImage2D` drops alpha, so glyph cells were solid green squares. The
531	  wrapper premultiplies the texture as it uploads and has `glColor4f` scale its
532	  colour: an additive blend cannot tell the difference. `xlockmore.h` must come
533	  before the `#define glTexImage2D` (it brings in `glshim.h`, whose macro would
534	  win). `matrix3.png` is deflated by `gl_textures.py` (`--deflate`). The step
535	  grows as the rain fills the screen (9 to 140 ms over about 80 s at full size)
536	  and fill is 100 of 145 ms: it renders at half size (`-DGLMATRIX_FULL` keeps
537	  full size) with `*density: 12` (26 strips, not 44) and `*delay: 10000`, about
538	  17 fps once full. Single precision gave byte-identical frames and about 3 ms.
539	  Upstream's brightness wave index runs 1 to `WAVE_SIZE` and the table has
540	  `WAVE_SIZE` entries, so a zero remainder read the next screen's state, a
541	  glyph at a junk brightness now and then (the trail review found it);
542	  `tools/glmatrix_patch.py` wraps it to 0, the brightest entry, which follows 1
543	  in the cycle. Its test compiles the hack's own statement over every row and
544	  wave position.
545	  The vertex alpha is clamped to 1 (`hacks/fold_alpha.h`, tested directly): a
546	  spinner glyph gets 1.5 times its brightness, and TinyGL masks a channel past
547	  full instead of saturating it, so a reproduced alpha of 1.087 gave green 5/63
548	  and the leading glyphs went dark (a trail review finding). A frame metric
549	  could not see it (a handful of pixels), so the helper is a plain header.
550	  Its texture setup also packs `a << 24` with an `unsigned char` promoted to a
551	  signed `int`, which overflows for an alpha of 128 or more (a sanitizer sweep
552	  found it): the patch widens it to `unsigned long`, the same bits.
553	- Cubenetic (`cubenetic_single_gl.c`, `tools/cubenetic_patch.py`) works out a
554	  256 by 256 plasma texture every frame, a square root per wave per pixel: 847
555	  ms a step, 1.2 fps. At 64 by 64 (`-DCUBENETIC_TEXTURE_SIZE`) it is 12-18 fps.
556	  The restart leak test found that `free_cube` never frees the cube array
557	  (320 bytes a start); the wrapper frees it. It passes the addresses of
558	  `double` locals to `get_position` and `get_rotation`, so it has the adapters
559	  HexTrail has.
560	- Superquadrics and Menger draw every face as a `GL_POLYGON`, which TinyGL
561	  drew as nothing until ARS-18 (both were black, and each wrapper mapped it
562	  to a triangle fan). Both render at half size
563	  (`-DSUPERQUADRICS_FULL`, `-DMENGER_FULL`); Superquadrics is single precision
564	  (13 to 19 fps, 8 to 11 before). Menger's depth 3 is 36,000 triangles and 920
565	  ms a frame, so the registry caps `*maxDepth` at 2 (11 to 44 fps, the low end
566	  while a level's display list is built).
567	- DeepStars was dropped after Rod saw it: about three dim stars on screen and
568	  no smear. Its source, notices row and `deepstars_gl.c` stay, the wrapper out
569	  of the build filter. The wrapper draws each smear copy at a lower alpha
570	  folded into the colour (TinyGL's blend is right only for black and white,
571	  so the blend is never enabled) and swallows `glEnable(GL_POINT_SMOOTH)`,
572	  which TinyGL warns about every frame. Upstream's stars are colours 0.15 to
573	  0.45 and 0.5 to 3 pixels across, so with no smooth points or real alpha they
574	  are faint and few, and `smear` only starts to grow after a random 1 in 800
575	  frames. It grows to 400 copies of 2,700 stars, 3.4 fps at 20, so the
576	  registry capped it at 4 (`*smear: 0.01`, now gone). To bring it back, add its
577	  registry entry (with that override), expected name, pin and leak test again.
578	- Circuit (`circuit_gl.c`, ARS-55) is the first port to lean on the TinyGL
579	  `GL_POLYGON` fan (ARS-18): its seven-segment display is `GL_POLYGON`
580	  hexagons, so it needs no `glBegin` wrapper, and a test counts pure-red pixels
581	  over a run (3,166 at most; nothing else it draws is pure red). The first
582	  host run aborted in the 3,000-frame test on two over-reads (see `gl.md`).
583	  `free_circuit` never frees the components still on the board, up to ten, so
584	  every stop leaked them: the wrapper frees them (payload, a diode's band, the
585	  component) before upstream's free, and the leak test fails without it. At
586	  full size on the board, over 240 s pinned: 8.4-11.4 fps (mean 9.7), step
587	  60-93 ms growing as components arrive, push 24.8 ms (every frame is a
588	  full push: the grid fills the screen), no wait, PSRAM flat. `gl_budget.py`
589	  predicted 79-85 ms a frame (12 fps) against about 103 measured (step plus
590	  push). It counts lines as free, and they are not (below).
591	  A single-precision build (ARS-55, committed and reverted: `b32fe24`,
592	  `bc549b2`) took `tools/softdouble_report.py`'s count in the wrapper's object
593	  from 198 call sites to 14 (the hack has no `double` keyword; its literals,
594	  `0.02` and `0.84`, were the cause) with host frames byte-identical, and moved
595	  the board by nothing: double and float alternated over two rounds, 28
596	  windows each, 9.76 vs 9.79 fps and a 77.6 vs 77.3 ms step. A `-DGL_PROFILE`
597	  build says why. Of a mean 79.8 ms step, 40.0 ms is the 156 lines of the
598	  board's grid (0.256 ms a line, every frame), 15.0 ms is the full-screen
599	  clear (the grid fills the box), about 18 ms is vertex setup, lighting,
600	  triangles and fills (growing from 1 ms to 32 ms as components arrive), and
601	  the hack's own code is 6.3 ms: the most any arithmetic change could win is
602	  8 percent. The lever is the grid's lines, not Circuit's maths.
603	  `-DCIRCUIT_HALF` renders at half the width and height
604	  (`glshim_set_render_scale(2)`, as Menger does). Alternating it with full
605	  size on the board, two rounds each (about 57 windows a build): full 9.67
606	  fps (8.4-11.6, step 78.6 ms), half 14.78 fps (13.0-18.4, step 42.1 ms); the
607	  push is 24.9 ms either way. Rod found the half-size picture noticeably
608	  blocky against the fine grid lines (2-pixel lines, chunky resistor bands and
609	  display dot), so it is opt-in, not the default. It leaves 217 KB more PSRAM
610	  free (6,049,231 against 5,832,095; `psram=` is free memory, and an earlier
611	  note here said the opposite). A scale-2 hack cannot overlap its push, so the
612	  registry flags Circuit `repaints_all` only without `-DCIRCUIT_HALF`.
613	  The flag earned its place narrowly. Pinned, alternating with
614	  `-DPUSH_NO_OVERLAP`, two rounds each (about 57 windows a build): plain 9.50
615	  fps (step 80.5 ms, push 24.8 ms), overlapped 10.29 fps (step 97.2 ms, push
616	  0.1 ms), +8.3 percent; window by window the ratio averaged 1.08 (0.98 to
617	  1.14). The step grew 17 ms, three times the usual 5, because both cores
618	  contend for the PSRAM cache and Circuit's lines are miss-heavy (a cache
619	  simulation of its real line pixels gives about 33,000 misses a frame, 1.1
620	  us each, which matches the 40 ms), so the 25 ms push hid only 8 of its
621	  milliseconds. It also takes 8.7 KB of internal heap.
622	  Line batching (see `gl.md`) then took the registered build from 10.59 to
623	  13.55 fps over two alternating rounds (step 93.2 to 72.3 ms, worst window
624	  9.2 to 11.6, best 16.2), with frames byte-identical. That is full size and
625	  crisp, but still under the 15 fps bar. The profile has not been taken again
626	  with batching on; before it, the clear was 15 ms and vertex setup, lighting
627	  and fills about 18 ms of the step.
628	- Phosphor (`phosphor_tty.c`, ARS-58) is an unmodified `phosphor.c` and
629	  `ansi-tty.c` behind a wrapper. Upstream reads a program on a pty
630	  (`xscreensaver-text`); the wrapper renames the `textclient_*` calls to a
631	  text source of its own (`phosphor_text.h`, tested directly): it `cat`s one
632	  of eleven public-domain poems, picked at random and never the one just shown,
633	  typed a character a frame. The shared `textclient.h` stays a NULL source,
634	  which XMatrix relies on. `firmware/assets/phosphor-poems.txt` is the source
635	  text; `tools/make_phosphor_poems.py` word-wraps it to 18 columns (4 in, the
636	  columns the round panel shows on rows 2 to 13: the corners of the 25 by 15
637	  grid are off the glass) and makes two headers. The default
638	  (`phosphor_poems_scroll.h`) types into a scroll region over rows 4 to 13 and
639	  scrolls there. `-DPHOSPHOR_PAGED` (`phosphor_poems.h`) pages instead: a page
640	  ends with `--More--`, a pause byte (`\001`) and a clear. Scrolling leaves a
641	  ghost of every character it moves under the new text (upstream's long
642	  sustain), which Rod preferred. Only poems published before 1931 go in
643	  (`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`); This Is Just To Say (1934) and This Be The Verse
644	  (1971) are still in copyright. The cursor blinks: upstream does it with Xt
645	  timers, which the shim never fires, so the wrapper maps `XtAppAddTimeOut` and
646	  `XtRemoveTimeOut` to a four-slot queue (`phosphor_timers.h`) that
647	  `phosphor_draw_blinking` fires once a draw (two thirds of a second on, a
648	  third off, restarting when the cursor moves). The wrapper overrides
649	  `*phosphorScale` to 3 (upstream's 6 is a 12 by 7 grid on 466 pixels) and
650	  `*cache: False` (a cache of every fade of every glyph is about 20 MB). The
651	  builtin 6 by 10 font is `images/gen/6x10font_png.h`, a blob made by
652	  `make_logo_blob.py --deflate` (1.3 KB). Upstream's glow is a fill through a
653	  clip mask, which `XFillRectangle` ignores, so the wrapper maps it to
654	  `xshim_fill_rect_clipped`: making the shared call honour the mask moved
655	  Bubbles' and Pacman's pinned frames, and without any such fill every
656	  letter was a solid cell (`test_phosphor_draws_letters_not_solid_cells`).
657	  Upstream's free leaves the tty grid, the Xft handle, three of its four
658	  glyph sets' structs and the first font pass's three GCs (it runs the pass
659	  twice and overwrites its GCs); the wrapper frees all of them. On the board
660	  with scrolling: 10.6-17.6 fps (mean 11.8), step 1.6-39.9 ms and push up to
661	  10.3 ms (a scroll redraws every cell: about 260 rows a frame); paged was
662	  13.0-17.6 (mean 16.2). `ansi-tty.c` writes to `stderr` only with `debug_p`
663	  set, and on the board that expands to `_impure_ptr`, which the toolchain
664	  lacks: `blurb.h` gives the file a null `stderr` there. `pio test` and
665	  `pio run -e stopwatch` must not overlap: the test run clears shared build
666	  state and the flash fails with a missing `firmware.elf`. A test that sizes
667	  a hack's output must include the header the wrapper chose
668	  (`phosphor_poem_set.h`): the test included the paged one and every
669	  wrapper mutant looked killed because the baseline was failing. Run a
670	  mutation script's baseline first and stop if it fails.
671
